label: Resonator spectroscopy vs coupler flux
axes: A two-dimensional colour map, one panel per measured qubit (multi-qubit runs place panels on a sparse grid, so blank cells are normal). The horizontal axis is the coupler flux bias being swept, with a twin top axis restating the same sweep as the equivalent bias-line current. The vertical axis is the readout drive frequency. Colour is the demodulated readout amplitude, and in these archives the band reads dark (low transmitted amplitude on resonance), so the resonator appears as a continuous narrow band of one extreme tone against uniform background texture. Confirm that polarity from the panel itself rather than assuming dark means resonance. Each panel is overlaid with two dashed vertical lines and a star: one line marks the fitted extremum of the resonator-frequency-versus-flux curve, and the other line together with the star marks the flux bias the node intends to park the coupler at and the resonator frequency it claims at that bias.
correct_signature: A single dark trough runs continuously across the whole flux sweep, present in every column, with no stretch of columns where it dissolves into the background.

The trough is bracketed by brighter background both above and below it, so a closed resonance is visible rather than just one flank running off an edge; its width relative to the swept window carries no information and must not be scored.
The trough's darkest colour is clearly deeper than the pixel-to-pixel mottle of the surrounding background, so its centre can be traced by eye column by column.

The trough's frequency changes only gently and smoothly along the flux axis — a shallow continuous ripple, or very nearly a straight flat line — with column-to-column changes small compared with the band's own thickness and no discontinuous step between neighbouring columns.

Narrow one- or two-column vertical streaks may cut across the band where the coupler passes a spurious mode; on a trustworthy figure the band resumes at the same frequency on both sides of each streak rather than being displaced by it.
Only one trough of this depth is present; there is no second, equally dark band of comparable continuity competing for the identification.
The star and its dashed line fall inside the plotted flux range, and the star's height coincides with the centre of the dark band in that column rather than sitting in bright background.

failure_appearance.no_signal: Observed only in a weak form: the swept frequency window does not contain a closed resonance, so instead of a narrow band the panel shows a broad dark slab occupying much of its height, or a single flank shading smoothly from bright to dark with no return to brighter background on the far side. There is no narrow continuous trace whose centre can be followed. A completely featureless panel with no dark structure at all was not observed in the archive.
failure_appearance.noisy: Strong pixel-to-pixel mottle across the whole panel; the background is speckled rather than smoothly graded and the band's edges are ragged and jump up and down by a fraction of the band's own width from one column to the next. The trough is still traceable as a continuous darker corridor, but in places its depth is comparable to the amplitude of the surrounding speckle, and isolated background pixels are as dark as the band itself.
failure_appearance.feature_present_fit_failed: The band itself is textbook — narrow, continuous across every column, deep against a smooth background, unambiguous to the eye — yet the panel carries no star and no claim line anywhere, because the claimed parking flux lies outside the swept flux range and so was never drawn. The figure therefore supports the existence of a resonator but offers nothing that ties the node's numeric claim to the measured data. The same class covers a star drawn at a height clearly outside the dark corridor while a clean band is plainly visible elsewhere.

abstain_when: The band's variation along the flux axis is smaller than the mottle or the pixel height, so it reads as a flat line. The figure then confirms only that a resonator is present; where along the flux axis any extremum sits is not visually determinable, so neither endorse nor reject a claim about the parking flux.
Only one flank of the trough is inside the frequency window, with no brighter background on both sides, so the band's centre cannot be located and any frequency claim is uncheckable from the picture.
No star or claim line is drawn and you cannot tell whether this plotting version draws one at all, so a missing marker cannot be distinguished from a marker that was never part of the figure.
The figure holds several panels and it is not clear from the picture which panel the numeric claim belongs to.
The colour scale is saturated so most of the panel is a single flat colour, or the band is clipped against the top or bottom edge of the frequency window.
The two dashed vertical lines are not distinguishable from one another in the picture, so anchor every judgement on the star rather than on which line is which.
notes: Thin and one-sided evidence. Every archived run of this family reports a successful fit and no node-rejected run exists, so the wrong-peak appearance was never observed and is left null rather than invented; the closest observed defect is a clean band whose claim marker fell outside the swept range, which is filed under feature-present-fit-failed. Drift is left null on principle, not for lack of looking: a single map visits each flux setting once and in order, so a slow monotonic wander of the band is indistinguishable from a genuine dependence on flux, and no figure of this family can separate the two. The single most important calibration for a judge here: because the coupler is only weakly coupled to the readout resonator, a nearly flat band is the NORMAL and healthy appearance in most runs. This is the opposite expectation from the qubit-flux version of the experiment, where a strong periodic arc is required; reading a flat band here as absence of response is the main way a judge will produce a false rejection. Two archived runs were zoomed so tightly in frequency that no closed trough fit in the window, which is what the no-signal entry describes; those panels still carry markers and still passed the node, so the judge should treat that appearance as uncheckable rather than as proof of a bad claim. Narrow vertical dropout streaks crossing the band recur across several archived runs and are not failures. Finally, the claimed frequency is specified far more precisely than the map can resolve, so only a gross mismatch — the star sitting visibly outside the dark corridor — is checkable from the picture; small offsets between the star and the band centre must not be treated as evidence against the claim. Marker semantics were confirmed by matching the drawn line positions against the stored fit fields across six runs, not assumed from the plot alone.
